lesson.intro: Linked list problems test whether you can move pointers without losing anything: rewire one pointer in the wrong order and half the list is gone. A few moves solve most interview questions: save, rewire, advance; the dummy head; fast and slow pointers; a fixed gap.
objectives: Trace pointer changes and predict the resulting list
Reverse, merge and delete in place with a dummy head
Find middles, cycles and the nth node from the end
Chain moves to solve palindrome and reorder problems
State each pattern's cost and the edge cases to test

sections.title: Nodes, pointers and the head
sections.key: A singly linked list is reachable only through its head: each node holds a value and a `next` pointer, so walk it with a separate `curr` pointer.
sections.body:
Picture a scavenger hunt: each clue holds a message plus the location of the next clue, so you cannot jump straight to clue 7. In a singly linked list each **node** stores a value and a **next** pointer; the last node's next is `None` (`null` in JavaScript).

[[visual]]

You are handed the **head**, the first node. Overwrite your only reference to it and the list is gone. Walking (start at the head, follow `next` until `None`) is the move every pattern builds on.

[[visual 2]]

Interviewers love linked lists because they test pointer discipline: changing references in the right order, handling empty and one-node lists, returning the right head. Real systems use them too: an LRU cache pairs a hash map with a doubly linked list.

visual.title: Linked list or array?
rows: Insert or delete at the front
Insert or delete after a node you hold
A pointer per node; two in a **doubly linked list**, which adds `prev`

sections.code:
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next

def build(values):                # Python list -> linked list head
    dummy = ListNode()
    tail = dummy
    for v in values:
        tail.next = ListNode(v)
        tail = tail.next
    return dummy.next

def to_list(head):
    out = []
    curr = head                   # never walk with head itself
    while curr:                   # stop when we fall off the end
        out.append(curr.val)
        curr = curr.next          # advance
    return out

head = build([1, 2, 3])
print(to_list(head), head.next.next.val)   # [1, 2, 3] 3
sections.tip: Make `curr = curr.next` the last line of a traversal loop and check it is there before you run anything. Forgetting it is the most common infinite loop in linked list code.
sections.pitfall: Walking with `head = head.next` destroys your only reference to the start of the list. Use a separate `curr` variable and leave `head` alone.

check.question: You hold a reference to node B in the singly linked list A -> B -> C -> D. Which operation is O(1)?
choices: Find the node that comes just before B
Insert a new node right after B
Read the value of the last node
Count how many nodes come after B
check.explanation: Inserting after B only changes B.next and the new node's next. Finding B's predecessor means walking from the head, because singly linked nodes have no prev pointer, and reaching the last node or counting the rest means walking to the end.

sections.title: Reversing a list: save, rewire, advance
sections.key: Reverse in place with three moves per node, in order: save `curr.next`, rewire `curr.next = prev`, advance both pointers. Then return `prev`, the new head.
sections.body:
Reverse `1 -> 2 -> 3` into `3 -> 2 -> 1`. You cannot reach the end directly, and you do not need to: if every arrow points backward, the list is reversed.

Walk with `prev` (the reversed part, starting as `None`) and `curr` (the node being processed). For each node:

- **Save:** `nxt = curr.next`, your only path to the rest of the list.
- **Rewire:** `curr.next = prev`.
- **Advance:** `prev = curr`, then `curr = nxt`.

[[visual]]

When `curr` falls off the end, `prev` is the old tail, now the head. Return `prev`, not `head`. Each node is touched once: O(n) time, O(1) space.

The recursive version reverses the rest, then hooks the head onto the end. It uses O(n) call stack, so Python's default limit of about 1000 frames crashes it on long lists.
sections.code:
def reverse_list(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next     # save
        curr.next = prev    # rewire
        prev = curr         # advance
        curr = nxt
    return prev             # the new head

def reverse_recursive(head):
    if head is None or head.next is None:
        return head
    new_head = reverse_recursive(head.next)  # reverse the rest
    head.next.next = head                    # the next node points back
    head.next = None                         # head becomes the tail
    return new_head
sections.tip: Draw three boxes labeled prev, curr and nxt, and move them one step at a time. Interviewers expect you to trace pointer code out loud.
sections.pitfall: Writing `curr.next = prev` before saving `curr.next` loses the rest of the list: after the first iteration `curr` has nowhere to go.

activity.title: Rewire the arrows
activity.prompt: Reverse the list one pointer at a time. Before each change, say which node you must save first and why. Notice that after every step the list is split into a reversed part and an untouched part.

check.question: When the loop in `reverse_list` finishes on `1 -> 2 -> 3`, what are `prev` and `curr`?
choices: prev is node 1 and curr is None
prev is None and curr is node 3
prev is node 3 and curr is None
prev is node 2 and curr is node 3
check.explanation: The loop runs until curr falls off the end, so curr is None. The last node processed was 3, which became prev, and that is why the function returns prev. Node 1, the old head, is now the tail.

sections.title: The dummy head: merging and deleting without special cases
sections.key: A dummy head is a throwaway node before the real head, so attaching or deleting at the head needs no special case; return `dummy.next`.
sections.body:
To merge `1 -> 3 -> 5` and `2 -> 4`, compare the front nodes, attach the smaller and advance that list. The first attach is awkward: the result has no head yet.

A **dummy head** (sentinel) removes that `if`: create a throwaway node, keep a `tail` at the end of the result, always attach to `tail.next`, and return `dummy.next`.

[[visual]]

When one list runs out, attach the rest of the other in one step. Merging reuses the nodes: O(n + m) time, O(1) extra space.

Use a dummy whenever the head might change: merging, building, deleting, or partitioning (two dummies joined at the end, then `None`).

**Deleting** works through the node **before** the target. Start `prev` at the dummy. If `prev.next` holds x, skip it with `prev.next = prev.next.next` and stay put: the new `prev.next` may hold x too.
sections.tip: Compare with `<=` so equal values keep their original order. The merge stays stable, which matters when nodes carry more than a number.
sections.pitfall: Returning `dummy` instead of `dummy.next` puts a stray 0 at the front of your answer.

activity.title: Merge two sorted lists
activity.prompt: Solve it with a dummy head and a tail pointer. Before you submit, check your code mentally against an empty list on either side.

check.question: In `remove_value`, why does the loop not advance `prev` right after deleting a node?
choices: Advancing would skip the dummy head, which must be returned
The node now after prev has not been checked yet and might also hold x
prev.next is always None after a deletion, so advancing would crash
Deleting a node already moves prev forward by itself
check.explanation: After prev.next = prev.next.next, prev.next is a node nobody has examined. With 1 -> 2 -> 2 -> 3 and x = 2, advancing after the first deletion would step onto the second 2 and never remove it.

sections.title: Fast and slow pointers: middles and cycles
sections.key: Move slow one step and fast two. When fast reaches the end, slow is in the middle; if the list has a cycle, fast eventually lands on slow.
sections.body:
Two runners start together, one twice as fast. When the fast one finishes, the slow one is halfway: the middle, found in one pass.

[[visual]]

For an even length, slow ends on the second middle node; loop `while fast.next and fast.next.next` for the first.

A **cycle** is a `next` pointing back to an earlier node, so a plain walk never ends. With two speeds, fast either reaches the end (no cycle) or, inside the cycle, gains exactly one node per step, so it cannot jump over slow: they meet.

This is **Floyd's cycle detection**: O(n) time, O(1) space. A set of visited nodes also works, but costs O(n) space.

**Where the cycle starts:** after they meet, move one pointer back to the head and step both one node at a time. They meet again at the cycle's first node.

visual.title: Finding the middle of five nodes
visual.caption: Now `fast.next` is `None`, so the loop stops with slow on 3, the middle.

sections.code:
def middle_node(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:     # fast can take two more steps
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    return slow

def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:          # the same node, not just equal values
            return True
    return False
sections.pitfall: Write the loop condition as `fast and fast.next`, in that order. Checking `fast.next` first crashes with AttributeError as soon as `fast` is already None.

activity.title: Find where the cycle starts
activity.prompt: The list 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 has its last node pointing back to node 2. Fill in the second phase of `cycle_start`: after the pointers meet, restart one of them at the head and step both one node at a time until they meet again. It should print 2. Then point node 5 at node 4 instead and check that it prints 4.

props.code:
class ListNode:
    def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
        self.val = val
        self.next = next

# Build 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5, then point 5 back at 2 to make a cycle.
nodes = [ListNode(v) for v in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]]
for a, b in zip(nodes, nodes[1:]):
    a.next = b
nodes[-1].next = nodes[1]
head = nodes[0]

def cycle_start(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            # They met inside the cycle. Move one pointer back to head,
            # then step both one node at a time until they meet again.
            # your code here
            return None
    return None   # no cycle

node = cycle_start(head)
print(node.val if node else "no cycle")
props.task: Complete cycle_start so it prints the value of the first node in the cycle: 2.

check.question: On the list `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6`, which node does `middle_node` return?
choices: 3 or 4, depending on the values
check.explanation: Fast moves 1, 3, 5 and then off the end, while slow moves 1, 2, 3, 4. With an even length this template lands on the second middle node. Loop while fast.next and fast.next.next if you want the first middle (3).

sections.title: A fixed gap: the nth node from the end
sections.key: Move fast n steps ahead, then move both until fast is on the last node: slow stops just before the nth node from the end, in one pass.
sections.body:
Remove the 2nd node from the end of `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5`, leaving `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 5`. Two passes work (count the length, then walk); the follow-up asks for one.

Open a fixed **gap**: move `fast` n steps ahead, then move both until `fast.next` is `None`. The gap never changes, so `slow` stops one node before the target, and `slow.next = slow.next.next` removes it.

[[visual]]

Start both at a dummy. When n equals the length, the head is the target: `slow` never leaves the dummy, and `dummy.next` skips the old head.

One pass: O(L) time, O(1) space. The big O matches two passes, but one pass also works on a stream you can read only once. It is the linked list cousin of a fixed-size window.

visual.title: Removing the 2nd from the end

rows.label: both move until fast.next is None

visual.caption: D is the dummy. The gap of 2 never changes, so slow stops right before the node to remove.

sections.code:
def remove_nth_from_end(head, n):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    slow = fast = dummy
    for _ in range(n):            # open a gap of n nodes
        fast = fast.next
    while fast.next:              # walk until fast is on the last node
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next
    slow.next = slow.next.next    # slow is just before the target
    return dummy.next

print(to_list(remove_nth_from_end(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), 2)))   # [1, 2, 3, 5]
print(to_list(remove_nth_from_end(build([1, 2, 3]), 3)))         # [2, 3]
print(to_list(remove_nth_from_end(build([7]), 1)))               # []
sections.tip: Before you code, test your loop bounds out loud on the smallest cases: one node with n = 1, and n equal to the length.
sections.pitfall: Stopping when `fast` is None (instead of when `fast.next` is None) leaves `slow` on the target itself, and a singly linked list cannot delete a node from that position.

check.question: In `remove_nth_from_end` with the dummy, n equals the list's length. Where does `slow` stop?
choices: On the head, so the second node is removed
On the last node, so nothing is removed
Nowhere: fast runs off the end and the code crashes
On the dummy node, so the head is removed
check.explanation: Moving fast n steps from the dummy puts it on the last node, so the while loop never runs. slow stays on the dummy and dummy.next = head.next removes the head. Without a dummy this case needs its own if statement.

sections.title: Combining moves: palindromes and reordering
sections.key: Hard linked list problems chain basic moves: find the middle, reverse the second half, then compare (palindrome) or weave (reorder), in O(1) extra space.
sections.body:
Is `1 -> 2 -> 2 -> 1` a palindrome? Copying the values into an array works, with O(n) space. The follow-up is always "now with O(1) extra space", and the answer chains moves you know:

[[visual]]

For `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1`, slow stops on 3. The reversed right half reads `1 -> 2 -> 3`, and comparing 3 with itself is harmless.

**Reorder list** turns `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5` into `1 -> 5 -> 2 -> 4 -> 3`: find the first middle, cut the list with `slow.next = None`, reverse the second half, then weave one node from each half in turn.

[[visual 2]]

Say each move out loud and write it as a small helper. Every step is O(n), so the whole is O(n) time and O(1) space.

steps.label: Reverse the second half in place
Compare the halves node by node
steps.detail: Stop when the reversed half runs out

steps.label: Reverse the second half again
steps.detail: Callers do not expect a check to scramble their list

visual.title: Reordering five nodes
visual.caption: After the cut and the reversal, take one node from each half in turn.

sections.code:
def is_palindrome(head):
    slow = fast = head                 # 1. find the middle
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    right = reverse_list(slow)         # 2. reverse the second half
    left, r, ok = head, right, True
    while r:                           # 3. compare
        if left.val != r.val:
            ok = False
            break
        left, r = left.next, r.next
    reverse_list(right)                # 4. restore the input
    return ok

def reorder_list(head):
    if head is None:
        return head
    slow = fast = head                 # first middle
    while fast.next and fast.next.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
    second = reverse_list(slow.next)
    slow.next = None                   # cut the list in two
    first = head
    while second:                      # weave
        a, b = first.next, second.next
        first.next = second
        second.next = a
        first, second = a, b
    return head

print(is_palindrome(build([1, 2, 3, 2, 1])))           # True
print(to_list(reorder_list(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]))))   # [1, 5, 2, 4, 3]
sections.pitfall: Forgetting to cut the list (`slow.next = None`) before weaving leaves the end of the first half pointing into the second half. The result contains a cycle, and printing it loops forever.

check.question: To check whether a linked list is a palindrome with O(1) extra space, which sequence of moves works?
choices: Reverse the whole list, then compare it with the original
Push every value onto a stack, then pop and compare
Find the middle, reverse the second half, compare the halves
Sort the nodes, then compare neighbors
check.explanation: Reversing the whole list in place destroys the original you wanted to compare against, and a stack or copy costs O(n) space. Reversing only the second half lets you compare the two halves directly with a constant number of pointers.

sections.title: Practice: spotting the pattern
sections.key: The input is a head node: match the wording to a move (reverse, dummy head, fast and slow, fixed gap, or middle plus reverse), then check the edge cases.
sections.body:
[[visual]]

Before you write code:

- Draw four or five nodes and label every pointer.
- Name the edge cases: empty list, one node, two nodes, a change at the head or the tail.
- Save `next` before you rewire it, and make every loop advance.
- Ask whether a dummy head would remove an `if`.
- Return the right node: `prev`, `dummy.next` or the head you saved.

Time is almost always O(n), since each node is visited a constant number of times. Space is where you stand out: O(1) for pointer solutions, O(n) if you copied values, used a set or recursed. Say which you wrote.

visual.title: Wording to move
rows: "merge", "partition", "remove all nodes that", the head may change
"middle", "cycle", "where does the loop begin", O(1) space
Two pointers with a fixed gap
Middle, reverse, then compare or weave
Two pointers that switch to the other list's head at the end, so both walk the same total distance

activity.title: Palindrome linked list
activity.prompt: Aim for O(1) extra space with the find middle, reverse, compare recipe. If you get stuck, solve it with an array first, pass the tests, then improve it.

check.question: A problem says: "Given the head of a list, return the node where its loop begins, using constant extra memory." Which pattern fits best?
choices: A dummy head and a single pass
Two pointers with a gap of n
Fast and slow pointers, then restart one pointer at the head
Reverse the list and compare it with the original
check.explanation: Floyd's algorithm finds a meeting point inside the cycle with fast and slow pointers. Restarting one pointer at the head and moving both one step at a time makes them meet at the cycle's first node, all in O(1) space. A visited set would also work, but it is not constant memory.

keyTerms.definition: One element of a linked list: a value plus a next pointer (and a prev pointer in a doubly linked list).
The first node. The only way to reach the rest of the list, so never lose your reference to it.
The reference from a node to the following node; None or null marks the end of the list.
A throwaway node placed before the real head so inserting or deleting at the head needs no special case. Return dummy.next.
The three steps of in-place reversal: store curr.next, point curr.next at prev, then move prev and curr forward.
Two pointers moving at one and two steps per iteration, used to find the middle and detect cycles in one pass.
The tortoise and hare algorithm: if fast and slow pointers ever meet, the list has a cycle. O(n) time, O(1) space.
Two pointers kept n nodes apart, so when the front one reaches the end, the back one is n nodes from the end.
A list whose nodes also point to the previous node, allowing O(1) deletion of a node you hold and walking backward.
A list where some node's next points back to an earlier node, so walking it never reaches None.

summary: A list is reachable only through its head; walk it with a separate `curr`.
Reverse with save, rewire, advance, and return `prev`.
A dummy head removes the special case when the head can change.
Fast and slow pointers find the middle and cycles; a fixed gap finds the nth from the end.
Hard problems chain moves: find the middle, reverse, then compare or weave.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend how to reverse a singly linked list in place: why you must save the next pointer before changing it, what prev and curr mean at each step, and why the function returns prev instead of head.

questions.question: Which operation is O(n) on a singly linked list but O(1) on an array?
choices: Reading the item at index i
Inserting a new first item
Deleting the first item
Checking whether the structure is empty
questions.explanation: An array computes the address of item i directly. A linked list has to follow i next pointers from the head. Inserting or deleting at the front is the opposite: O(1) for the list, O(n) for the array because everything shifts.

questions.question: What does this code print?
questions.code:
head = ListNode(5, ListNode(7, ListNode(9)))
print(head.next.val + head.next.next.val)
questions.explanation: head.next is the node holding 7 and head.next.next is the node holding 9, so it prints 7 + 9 = 16. The 5 in the head node is never read.

questions.question: `count_nodes` never returns when given a non-empty list. What is wrong?
choices: count should start at 1
The loop should test curr.next instead of curr
curr is never advanced, so the loop condition never becomes false
It should return count + 1
questions.explanation: Nothing inside the loop changes curr, so `while curr` stays true forever. Adding curr = curr.next as the last line of the loop fixes it. Starting count at 1 or testing curr.next would only give wrong counts.

questions.question: Put the steps of one iteration of in-place list reversal in order.
items: Save the next node: nxt = curr.next
Point the current node backward: curr.next = prev
questions.explanation: You must save curr.next before overwriting it, then flip the pointer, then move both pointers forward. Moving curr before prev would lose the node prev needs to become.

questions.question: Complete the JavaScript reversal so it returns the head of the reversed list.
choices: head
prev
curr
nxt
questions.explanation: When the loop ends, curr is null and prev is the old tail, which is now the first node. head still points at the old first node, which is now the last node, so returning head gives a one-node list.

questions.question: This reversal returns a list containing only the first node, whatever the input. What is wrong?
questions.code:
def reverse_list(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        curr.next = prev
        prev = curr
        curr = curr.next
    return prev
choices: curr.next is overwritten before it is saved, so curr = curr.next follows the new pointer instead
prev should start at head instead of None
The loop should be while curr.next
It should return curr instead of prev
questions.explanation: curr.next = prev overwrites the only pointer to the rest of the list. The last line then reads curr.next, which is now prev (None on the first pass), so the loop ends after one node. Save nxt = curr.next first.

questions.question: In Python, `reverse_recursive` works on a 500-node list but raises RecursionError on a 5,000-node list. Why?
choices: The recursive version is O(n^2), so it times out
Each node adds a stack frame, and Python's default limit is about 1000
Python cannot hold more than 1000 ListNode objects at once
head.next.next = head creates a cycle on long lists
questions.explanation: Each node adds one frame to the call stack, and Python's default recursion limit is about 1000 frames. The iterative version uses O(1) extra space and has no such limit. The recursive version is O(n) time, not O(n^2).

questions.question: Why do so many linked list solutions start with `dummy = ListNode()`?
choices: Python requires a node before the head of any list
It lets the algorithm run in O(log n) time
It stores the length of the list
Changes at the head need no special case
questions.explanation: The dummy gives the real head a node in front of it, so adding or removing at the head works exactly like everywhere else. Return dummy.next at the end. It does not change the time complexity.

questions.question: Using `merge_two_lists` from this section, what does `to_list(merge_two_lists(build([1, 4]), build([2, 3, 6])))` return?
questions.explanation: Compare fronts: 1 vs 2 takes 1, 4 vs 2 takes 2, 4 vs 3 takes 3, 4 vs 6 takes 4. The first list is empty, so the rest of the second (6) is attached in one step.

questions.question: Called with `1 -> 5 -> 9` and `2 -> 3`, this merge returns `1 -> 2 -> 3`. What is missing?
choices: The comparison should be a.val < b.val
After the loop, attach the leftover nodes with tail.next = a or b
tail should start at the head of a
The loop should be while a or b
questions.explanation: When b runs out, the loop stops and the rest of a (5 -> 9) is never attached. tail.next = a or b after the loop fixes it. Changing the loop to while a or b would crash on a.val when a is None.

questions.question: In `remove_value(head, x)`, why does `prev` start at the dummy instead of at the head?
choices: Starting at the head would make the loop O(n^2)
The dummy holds the value x to compare against
A node is deleted through the node before it, and the head has none without a dummy
Python does not allow assigning to head.next
questions.explanation: A singly linked node is removed by changing the next pointer of the node before it. The head has no node before it unless you add a dummy, so starting at the dummy lets the head be deleted like any other node.

questions.question: In the fast and slow pointer pattern, how far does each pointer move per iteration?
choices: slow 1 node, fast 2 nodes
slow 1 node, fast n nodes
slow 2 nodes, fast 4 nodes
Both 1 node, with fast starting 2 ahead
questions.explanation: slow moves one node and fast moves two. When fast reaches the end, slow has covered half the distance, which is why it lands on the middle. A gap of n is a different pattern, used for the nth node from the end.

questions.question: Which value does `middle_node` return for `10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 40`?
questions.explanation: slow goes 10, 20, 30 while fast goes 10, 30 and then off the end (40.next is None). For even lengths this template returns the second middle, 30.

questions.question: This `has_cycle` crashes with AttributeError on some lists that have no cycle. Which lists, and why?
choices: Odd-length lists, because slow runs off the end first
Even-length lists, because fast becomes None and fast.next is read before fast is checked
Lists with duplicate values, because slow is fast compares values
One-node lists, because slow.next is None
questions.explanation: On an even-length list, fast jumps to None on its last move. The condition then evaluates fast.next before checking fast, and None has no next attribute. Writing `while fast and fast.next` checks fast first and short-circuits.

questions.question: Why does `has_cycle` compare `slow is fast` rather than `slow.val == fast.val`?
choices: is is faster, and the two checks always agree
val may be None in the last node
Different nodes can hold equal values, so equal values prove nothing
== cannot compare integers stored in objects
questions.explanation: Different nodes can hold equal values, so equal values do not prove the pointers are on the same node. `is` checks that both names refer to the very same object, which is what meeting inside a cycle means.

questions.question: A candidate detects a cycle by storing every visited node in a set. Compared with Floyd's algorithm, what is the trade-off?
choices: Same O(n) time, but O(n) extra space instead of O(1)
It is O(n^2) because set lookups are linear
It fails when two nodes hold the same value
It cannot detect a cycle that starts at the head
questions.explanation: A set of nodes gives O(n) time with average O(1) lookups, but it stores up to n references, so it needs O(n) extra space. Floyd's algorithm uses two pointers, O(1) space. Python sets of nodes hash by identity by default, so equal values do not confuse it.

questions.question: Put the steps for finding the first node of a cycle in order.
items: Move slow one step and fast two steps until they meet
Move one pointer back to the head
Advance both pointers one step at a time
Stop when they meet: that node is the start of the cycle
questions.explanation: Phase one finds a meeting point inside the cycle. Phase two resets one pointer to the head and moves both at the same speed; the distance from the head to the cycle start equals the distance from the meeting point to the cycle start (modulo the cycle length), so they meet there.

questions.question: In `remove_nth_from_end`, what happens before the two pointers start moving together?
choices: fast moves to the last node
fast moves to the middle with the fast and slow pattern
slow moves n steps ahead of fast
fast moves n steps ahead to open a gap
questions.explanation: fast moves n steps ahead, opening a gap of n nodes. Moving both at the same speed keeps that gap, so when fast is on the last node, slow is just before the node to delete.

questions.question: What list is left after `remove_nth_from_end(build([10, 20, 30, 40, 50]), 3)`? Type it as a Python list.
questions.explanation: The 3rd node from the end of a 5-node list is the 3rd node from the front, 30. The gap of 3 leaves slow on 20, and 20.next is pointed past 30 to 40.

questions.question: This version has no dummy node. Which call breaks it?
choices: n = 1 on 1 -> 2 -> 3, because the tail cannot be removed
n = 2 on 1 -> 2 -> 3, because slow stops on the wrong node
n = 3 on 1 -> 2 -> 3, because fast becomes None and fast.next crashes
Any even-length list, because the gap is off by one
questions.explanation: With n equal to the length, the for loop moves fast past the last node to None, and `while fast.next` raises AttributeError. Even if it did not crash, there is no node before the head to unlink it from. The dummy node fixes both problems.

questions.question: Counting the length and then walking again is O(L), and so is the gap method. What does the gap method actually buy you?
choices: It reads the list only once, which helps with streams or a one-pass requirement
It lowers the time to O(log L)
It uses O(1) space where the two-pass version needs O(L)
It removes the need for a dummy head
questions.explanation: Both are O(L) time and O(1) space. The gap method reads the list once, which matters when you can only read it once (a stream) or when the interviewer explicitly asks for one pass. It does not change the big O.

questions.question: Put the steps of the O(1) space palindrome check in order.
items: Find the middle with fast and slow pointers
Reverse the second half in place
Compare the first half with the reversed second half
Reverse the second half again to restore the list
questions.explanation: You need the middle before you can reverse the second half, and you need the reversed half before you can compare. Restoring comes last so the caller gets their list back unchanged.

questions.question: What does `reorder_list` from this section produce for `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5 -> 6`? Type it as a Python list.
questions.explanation: The first middle is 3, so the halves are 1 -> 2 -> 3 and 4 -> 5 -> 6. Reversing the second gives 6 -> 5 -> 4, and weaving one node from each gives 1, 6, 2, 5, 3, 4.

questions.question: Why does `reorder_list` set `slow.next = None` before weaving the halves together?
choices: To free the memory used by the second half
The first half would still point into the second half and the result would contain a cycle
reverse_list only works on lists that end in a cycle
To make the first half shorter than the second
questions.explanation: Without the cut, the last node of the first half still points into the second half. Weaving then creates a loop in the result, and anything that walks it never ends.

questions.question: Copying a list's values into a Python list and checking `vals == vals[::-1]` solves the palindrome problem. What does it cost?
choices: O(n) time and O(1) extra space
O(n log n) time and O(n) extra space
O(n^2) time and O(1) extra space
O(n) time and O(n) extra space
questions.explanation: Copying is one O(n) pass, reversing and comparing are O(n) more, and the copy holds n values. That is O(n) time and O(n) space, which is why interviewers ask for the O(1) space version.

questions.question: Match each problem with the linked list move that solves it.

pairs.left: Find the node where a loop begins
Delete the 4th node from the end in one pass
pairs.right: Two pointers with a fixed gap

pairs.left: Merge two sorted lists into one
pairs.right: Dummy head with a tail pointer

questions.explanation: Cycle start needs fast and slow pointers plus a restart. The nth from the end in one pass needs a fixed gap. Merging builds a new chain, which a dummy head simplifies. Reversal is save, rewire, advance.

questions.question: Which inputs should you test for almost every linked list function? Select all that apply.
choices: An empty list (head is None)
A list with a single node
A case where the head node itself changes or is removed
A list with more than a million nodes
A list whose values are sorted in descending order
questions.explanation: Empty lists, one-node lists and changes at the head are where pointer code usually breaks: None checks, loops that never run, and a head that has no previous node. Huge or descending inputs rarely reveal pointer bugs.

questions.question: Why do interviewers keep asking linked list questions when most production code never builds a linked list by hand?
questions.answer: They test pointer discipline: updating references in the right order without losing nodes, handling the empty, one-node and head-changing cases, and reasoning about O(1) versus O(n) extra space.
questions.explanation: The data structure is simple, so all the difficulty is in the pointer handling, which shows how carefully a candidate reasons about state.

questions.question: Two lists merge into a shared tail. Pointer A walks list A and then jumps to list B's head; pointer B does the reverse. Why do they meet at the first shared node?
choices: The shorter list is padded with dummy nodes first
One pointer moves two steps per turn and catches the other
They compare values and stop at the first equal pair
Both walk the same total distance, so they line up at the shared tail
questions.explanation: If list A has a nodes before the shared part, list B has b, and the shared tail has c, pointer A walks a + c + b steps to reach the junction and pointer B walks b + c + a. The distances are equal, so they arrive together. If there is no shared node, both reach None at the same time.

questions.question: Rearrange a list so nodes with values below x come first and the rest follow, keeping the original order inside each group. Which plan is O(n) time and O(1) extra space?
choices: Swap values between nodes like the quicksort partition step
Sort the list with merge sort and cut it at x
Reverse the list, then split it at the first value of at least x
Append each node to one of two dummy lists, then join them and end with None
questions.explanation: Two dummies collect the two groups in order, then the "less" chain is joined to the first real node of the other chain, and the final tail must be set to None or the old next pointer can create a cycle. Swapping values like quicksort does not keep the original order.
